PHYSICAL FOUNDATIONS

A Mechanical Disturbance in an Elastic Medium

Sound is not an object; it is a traveling mechanical pressure oscillation. Vibrating matter pushes and pulls surrounding gas molecules, forming alternating compressions and rarefactions that propagate at 343 meters per second.

VARIABLE DEFINITIONS & SI UNITS

B Bulk Modulus Pa (N/m2) Elastic resistance of substance to uniform volumetric compression

PHYSICAL RELATIONSHIP & PROPORTIONALITY
Stiffness vs. Inertia: Sound speed increases with elastic restoring force (B) and decreases with mass inertia (ρ).
Although water is 800 times denser than air, its bulk modulus is over 15,000 times higher (B ≈ 2.18 × 109 Pa). As a result, sound travels over 4.3 times faster in cochlear perilymph fluid (1,480 m/s) than in atmospheric air!
Thermal Kinetic Effect: Warmer air molecules possess higher kinetic energy, restoring pressure equilibrium faster and adding +0.606 m/s per degree Celsius.

BIOMECHANICAL TRANSDUCTION

The Middle Ear as an Impedance Transformer

Air is light; fluid is dense. When airborne sound strikes fluid, 99.9% reflects away. The middle ear bones form a physical 22x pressure amplifier that transfers sound into the inner ear without loss.

TONOTOPIC FOURIER ANALYSIS

Spatial Frequency Dispersion Along the Basilar Ribbon

Inside the temporal bone rests the cochlea — a 32 mm fluid channel partitioned by the basilar membrane. The cochlea acts as a biological Fourier analyzer, physically sorting frequencies by location.

PRECISION BIOACOUSTICS
Fig. 4.1: Bioacoustic research laboratory measuring cochlear traveling waves. Georg von Békésy was awarded the 1961 Nobel Prize for demonstrating how waves peak at distinct physical points along the basilar membrane.

Stiffness Gradients & Traveling Waves

Why do different frequencies peak at different places? The basilar membrane has physical gradients:

  • At the Base (near oval window): Narrow (0.1 mm), taut, and 100 times stiffer. Resonates to high frequencies (up to 20,000 Hz).
  • At the Apex (tip, helicotrema): Wide (0.5 mm), loose, and compliant. Resonates to low frequencies (down to 20 Hz).
GRADE 11 PHYSICS · BIOMECHANICAL TONOTOPY & LOGARITHMIC MAPS

Computes the characteristic resonant frequency of each microscopic point along the 35 mm human basilar membrane, establishing the biomechanical foundation for cochlear implants.

f(x) = A × ( 10a·x − k )
Human Calibration: f(x) = 165.4 × (100.060 · x − 0.88)
Inverse Map (Position from Pitch): x(f) =
10.060
× log10
f165.4
+ 0.88
VARIABLE DEFINITIONS & SI UNITS
SymbolQuantityStandard Human ValuePhysical Meaning
x Basilar Distance 0 to 35 mm Metric distance along the uncoiled cochlea from apex (0 mm) to base (35 mm)
f(x) Resonant Frequency Hz (20 to 20,000 Hz) Acoustic pitch exciting maximum traveling wave basilar excursion at x
A Scaling Constant 165.4 Hz Empirical human frequency scale factor (Greenwood, 1990)
a Stiffness Slope 0.060 mm-1 Exponential gradient of basilar membrane stiffness per millimeter

PHYSICAL RELATIONSHIP & PROPORTIONALITY
Exponential Stiffness Gradient: The basilar membrane is not uniform.
  • At the basal entrance (near the oval window), the membrane is narrow (0.1 mm) and extremely stiff.
  • At the apical tip, the membrane is 5 times wider (0.5 mm) and ~100 times more flexible.
Because mechanical resonance scales as f ∝
√
KM
, characteristic frequency drops exponentially with distance. Musical Pitch Linearity: Each musical octave occupies roughly 3.5 mm of basilar membrane length across the entire cochlea!
THREE-POINT AUDITORY BENCHMARK Verifying Apex, Speech Band, and Basal Extremes
1
Apical Resonance (x = 0 mm, Deep Cochlear Tip):
f(0) = 165.4 × (100 − 0.88) = 165.4 × (1.00 − 0.88) = 165.4 × 0.12 = 19.8 Hz ≈ 20 Hz (threshold of human hearing)
2
Mid-Cochlea Resonance (x = 17.5 mm, Vowel Formants):
f(17.5) = 165.4 × (100.060 × 17.5 − 0.88) = 165.4 × (101.05 − 0.88) = 165.4 × (11.22 − 0.88) = 1,710 Hz (speech formant range)
3
Basal Entrance (x = 35.0 mm, Stapes Interface):
f(35) = 165.4 × (100.060 × 35 − 0.88) = 165.4 × (102.10 − 0.88) = 165.4 × (125.89 − 0.88) = 20,677 Hz ≈ 20 kHz (ultrasound threshold)

Because of this physical map (called tonotopy), each pitch excites a specific bundle of auditory nerve fibers. The brain knows what frequency entered the ear simply by noting where the basilar membrane vibrated.

PATHOLOGY & NEUROPROSTHETICS

Acoustic Amplification vs. Direct Neural Stimulation

In sensorineural hearing loss, the microscopic hair cells inside the cochlea are damaged or dead. Turning up the volume with a hearing aid cannot restore missing biological switches — but a cochlear implant bypasses them completely.

CELLULAR MICROSCOPY
Fig. 5.1: Electron microscope facility examining inner ear hair cells. Humans possess ~15,000 hair cells per ear at birth, which do not regenerate once lost.

Mechanosensory Destruction

Perched atop each hair cell is a bundle of stereocilia, connected by tiny spring filaments called tip links (composed of cadherin-23 and protocadherin-15 proteins).

When the basilar membrane vibrates, stereocilia bend, pulling open mechanotransduction (MET) ion channels that admit K+ and Ca2+ ions to trigger nerve impulses. Acoustic trauma or illness shears these fragile tip links.

Once hair cells are gone, sound waves cannot create electrical voltage. A hearing aid simply amplifies acoustic waves into non-functioning receptors, producing distorted noise.

FIGURE 5.2 · MECHANOTRANSDUCTION ULTRASTRUCTURE

Healthy Mechanoreceptor vs. Acoustic Trauma Damage

STEREOCILIA BUNDLE (3-TIERED STAIRCASE)

Each hair cell carries 50–100 actin-filled stereocilia arranged in ascending height tiers. Mechanical fluid motion deflects the bundle toward the tallest kinocilium, placing tension on tip links.

Reference: Pickles, J. O. et al. (1984). Hearing Research, 15(3), 269–282.

STAGE 3: DIGITAL SIGNAL PROCESSOR (DSP)

Signal Domain: Digital Binary Floating-Point Computations

An ultra-low-power CMOS integrated circuit running on ~1 Volt. It splits audio into 16 to 48 independent frequency channels, applies customized gain curves matching the patient's audiogram, compresses loud sounds (WDRC) so they don't hurt, and cancels acoustic squeal (feedback).

CLINICAL THRESHOLDS

The Boundary for Implantation

A hearing aid is ideal when viable hair cells remain to detect amplified air pressure waves. But when hair cells are completely absent, acoustic gain cannot induce neural firing.

A cochlear implant introduces platinum-iridium electrodes directly into the perilymph fluid of the scala tympani, depolarizing spiral ganglion neurons with electrical voltage (V = I · R) and completely bypassing the non-functional mechanoreceptors.

SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE

The Six Transduction Stages of a Cochlear Implant

A cochlear implant is a true bionic neuroprosthesis. In under 2 milliseconds, it captures pressure oscillations in air, extracts acoustic spectral envelopes, beams digital code across intact skin via magnetic induction, and fires electrical currents into the auditory nerve.

How Cochlear Implants Work: Bionic Signal Transmission

Stage 01: Dual Microphone Array & Sound Processor

ENERGY DOMAIN: ACOUSTIC → ANALOG VOLTAGE

Miniature electret or MEMS omnidirectional microphones capture sound pressure waves behind the outer ear pinna. Adaptive directional algorithms filter out ambient reverberation and steer sensitivity toward conversation partners.

Processing latency: < 0.2 ms · Sampling: 16-44.1 kHz · Power: Zinc-air or Li-ion cell
BIOPHYSICAL CONSTRAINTS

Current Spread: Why 22 Electrodes Yield ~8 Effective Pitch Channels

Modern cochlear implants have 16 to 22 physical electrode contacts. However, because cochlear perilymph fluid is an electrical conductor, electrical current spreads outwards from each contact, exciting neighboring nerve fibers.

CENTRAL LABORATORY EXPERIMENT

The Channel Vocoder Simulator

How does human speech sound when filtered through the spatial bottleneck of a cochlear implant? Use this real-time DSP vocoder to decompose audio into discrete frequency bands, extract temporal envelopes, and reconstruct sound through noise or sine carriers.

SCIENTIFIC MONOGRAPH NOTE · ACOUSTIC APPROXIMATION

A channel vocoder is an acoustic model based on the psychoacoustic methods of Shannon et al. (1995) and Loizou (1999). It illustrates the reduction in spectral resolution and pitch structure that a newly implanted ear receives. However, it is an approximation: recipient brains undergo remarkable neuroplastic adaptation over months of rehabilitation, learning to extract rich linguistic meaning from these electrical pulse trains.

AUDIO SIGNAL PROCESSING
Fig. 7.1: Digital audio signal processing desk. The Shannon channel vocoder splits incoming speech into N logarithmic frequency bands, rectifies each band to extract its amplitude envelope (< 50 Hz), and uses that envelope to amplitude-modulate band-limited noise carriers.
GRADE 11 PHYSICS · INFORMATION THEORY & DIGITAL SIGNAL PROCESSING

Channel Vocoder Synthesis & Shannon Channel Capacity

Defines the mathematical summation used by cochlear neuroprosthetics to reconstruct acoustic speech and the theoretical information capacity of degraded neural channels.

svocoded(t) = ∑k=1N [ Envk(t) × Carrierk(t) ]
Shannon Capacity: C = B × log2 ( 1 +
SN
)
Envelope Extraction: Envk(t) = LPF160 Hz(|xk(t)|)
Electrode Count: N = 8 to 22 physical channels
VARIABLE DEFINITIONS & SI UNITS
SymbolQuantitySI UnitPhysical Meaning
C Channel Capacity bits/s Maximum theoretical error-free information rate through channel
B Acoustic Bandwidth Hz Frequency span of each discrete bandpass filter
S / N Signal-to-Noise Ratio dimensionless Ratio of neural signal power to background electrical crosstalk noise
Envk(t) Temporal Envelope dimensionless Slowly varying amplitude modulation (fc ≤ 160 Hz) carrying syllable rhythm
Carrierk(t) Carrier Signal acoustic wave Bandpassed acoustic noise or biphasic electrical pulse train for channel k
PHYSICAL RELATIONSHIP & PROPORTIONALITY
Envelope vs. Fine Structure: Spoken language comprehension relies overwhelmingly on low-frequency temporal envelopes (≤ 50 Hz rhythm, ≤ 160 Hz voicing cues) across 8 to 12 distinct spectral channels.
  • Because speech redundancy is so vast, 12 to 16 cochlear implant channels deliver more than enough Shannon capacity (> 20 kbps) for > 80% sentence recognition in quiet.
  • In contrast, musical harmony and pitch timbre demand microsecond-accurate acoustic fine structure (> 500 Hz phase locking) across hundreds of points, which discrete current pulses cannot yet replicate.
INFORMATION THEORY CALCULATION Quantifying Neural Information Flow Through an Electrode Array
1
Channel Parameters: Bandwidth B = 300 Hz per electrode, Signal-to-Noise ratio S/N = 31 (equivalent to +15 dB electrical SNR). Target: calculate single-channel capacity.
2
Apply Shannon-Hartley Theorem:
C = 300 × log2(1 + 31) = 300 × log2(32) = 300 × 5 = 1,500 bits/s
3
Aggregate 16-Electrode Neuroprosthetic Array Bandwidth:
Ctotal = 16 × 1,500 bits/s = 24,000 bits/s (24 kbps)
This 24 kbps information pipe exceeds the 100-200 bps linguistic entropy of conversational speech by two orders of magnitude, making fluent spoken dialogue possible!

THE FRONTIER OF NEUROPROSTHETICS

Why Music is Hard for Implants

While speech relies on slow temporal envelope changes (< 50 Hz) that 8 channels easily carry, music depends on fine harmonic pitch structure (Δf < 2 Hz). Channel vocoders smear sharp integer overtones into coarse noise bands, turning melodies into rhythmic percussive thumps.

HARMONIC ACOUSTICS
Fig. 9.1: String vibration and acoustic overtones. Musical pitch is defined by the fundamental frequency (f0) and integer harmonics (2f0, 3f0, 4f0). Discriminating two adjacent semitones requires resolving a ~6% change in frequency (≈ 1-2 Hz).
POLYPHONIC ORCHESTRA
Fig. 9.2: Symphonic polyphony. Multiple overlapping instruments produce dense spectral structures that require thousands of distinct frequency channels to resolve.

SYNTHESIS & SCHOLARLY SOURCES

Conclusions, Scholarly References, and Credits

The human ear and the cochlear implant represent two extraordinary physical solutions to the challenges of acoustic wave transduction and neural signaling.

PHYSICAL PRINCIPLE 01

Impedance Matching

The middle ear ossicles concentrate atmospheric wave force across a 17:1 area ratio and 1.3:1 lever advantage, achieving a 22-fold pressure gain that overcomes a 99.9% energy reflection barrier at the air-fluid cochlear boundary.

PHYSICAL PRINCIPLE 02

Tonotopic Dispersion

The cochlea performs spatial mechanical Fourier analysis. The narrow, taut base resonates to high frequencies up to 20,000 Hz, while the wide, compliant apex resonates to low frequencies down to 20 Hz, mapping frequency along 32 mm of neural space.

PHYSICAL PRINCIPLE 03

Current Spread & Vocoding

Speech intelligibility relies on slow temporal envelope modulations (< 50 Hz), which are intelligible with only 8 spectral channels. However, electrical current spread in conductive perilymph fluid limits pitch resolution, making music and noisy rooms challenging.
